newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, dollar weaker on data, bonds edge higher.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, dollar weaker on data, bonds edge higher.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks and the dollar fell Wednesday as news of a widening U.S. trade deficit in July raised doubts about the economy's strength and whether the Federal Reserve will need to raise interest rates.
Bonds edged higher.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 11.47 points at 5,877.36. In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,346 to 951 on moderate volume of 395 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index, which is laced with technology stocks, rose 2.40 to 1,205.71, nearing its June 5 record close of 1,249.15.

The big news was a Commerce Department report that the U.S. trade deficit ballooned by 42.6 percent in July to $11.68 billion from $8.19 billion in June. The magnitude of the deficit shocked economists, who had generally forecast a gap of $8.8 billion.

Analysts said the deficit, which was the largest since late 1987, threw into question just how robust a rate of growth the economy continues to enjoy and further muddied the near-term outlook for interest rates.

"If you're an economist, you worry a lot about this number because it says gross domestic product may be weaker than economists are forecasting for the third quarter," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.
Analysts said the weakness in U.S. exports was expected to prompt economists to lower their estimates of third-quarter economic growth.
The report was one of the final pieces of broad-based economic evidence before next Tuesday's meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee to review interest-rate strategy.
The Dow index soared nearly 230 points for last week and Monday, setting a record high of 5,889.20 on investors' hopes that the Fed would not raise short-term interest rates.
But on Tuesday, a Reuter report that suggested some Fed members were leaning toward a hike in the discount rate revived Wall Street's jitters that the cost of borrowing may be going up.
Technology stocks were boosted by Merrill Lynch's naming of International Business Machines Corp. to its 'Focus One' stock of the week.

"I believe my IBM earnings estimates are above consensus for the fourth quarter and if achieved, Wall Street will have greater confidence in 1997," said Daniel Mandresh, Merrill Lynch's computer industry analyst.
The 30-year Treasury bond rose 2/32, or 62.5 cents on a $1,000 bond, reducing its yield to 6.82 percent from 7.03 percent at Tuesday's close.
In late trading, the dollar stood at 1.5090 German marks, down from 1.5143 marks late Tuesday. The dollar fell to 109.12 Japanese yen from 110.35 yen.
Heating oil prices jumped on supply concerns after the American Petroleum Institute said heating oil inventories were still running at a significant deficit over last year.
Heating oil for October delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange settled up 2.28 cents to 67.87 cents a gallon after rising as high as 68.00 cents a gallon.
October crude oil closed up 58 cents to $23.89 a barrel. October gasoline closed up 0.32 cent to 63.06 cents a gallon.
Corn and wheat prices closed higher on signs of surprisingly strong commercial demand for grains despite upcoming harvest supplies.

At the Chicago Board of Trade September wheat closed 9-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $4.32-1/2, and September corn closed up 4-1/4 cents at $3.55-1/2. September soybeans gained 4-1/2 cents to $8.19-1/2.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 share index closed a lackluster trading session 16.6 points lower at 3,955.7, just off the day's lows. In Tokyo, the key Nikkei 225 average closed down 153.84 points at 21,156.75.
